prime.problem: A DP table over all n days, or a list of every person, grows without bound: at n = 1,000, delay = 1 the secret count has 301 digits, so a person-by-person simulation can't even be built. Re-summing the window each day costs O(n · forget).
prime.fits: Follows the monotonic deque: the same container, used here not to find an extreme but to hold exactly the last k DP values. It relies on the toolkit's O(1) append and popleft, and previews the rolling arrays of cs-3's DP cards.
expect: a recurrence that reads only the last forget days
append today, popleft the day that drops out
a running sum updated by two terms per day
appendleft for building output from the right (Integer to English Words)
prime.goal: Turn a recurrence that looks back a bounded number of steps into an O(n)-time, O(window)-memory loop, and trace People Aware of a Secret and Integer to English Words by hand.

attend: Why does share change by exactly two terms each day instead of being re-summed?
Why is the answer the sum of the deque, not its last value?
In Integer to English Words, why does each chunk go on the left?
When would a plain list used as a ring buffer beat the deque here?

must: Today's sharers = yesterday's + those who learned delay days ago − those who learned forget days ago → only the last forget values of new[] are ever read → keep them in a deque of length forget → O(forget) memory instead of O(n)
Each day: add new[t − delay], subtract the popleft'd new[t − forget], append today → three O(1) steps per day → O(n) time versus 499,500 additions to re-sum at n = 1,000
divmod(num, 1000) yields the lowest chunk first but it is read last → appendleft each chunk (O(1) on a deque) → no reversal or front inserts into a list
elevated: Deque indexing is O(1) near the ends but O(n) in the middle → new[-delay] with delay near forget/2 on a huge window isn't free → a ring buffer new[t % forget] is O(1) everywhere
Python ints don't overflow → the exact count is kept (301 digits) → LeetCode's version needs the answer mod 10⁹ + 7 because fixed-width languages would overflow

compress.prompt: From memory, write the three lines of the daily update and one sentence each on why the deque has length forget and why the answer is its sum. Then state the Integer to English Words trick in one sentence.
checklist: only the last forget days of learners are still sharing or still aware
aware = those who learned within the last forget days = sum of the deque
lowest thousand-chunk comes first, so appendleft puts it last

retrieve.q: Explain why this problem needs only a window of forget values, not a full DP table.
answer: the recurrence reads new[t − delay] and new[t − forget], both within the last forget days
people who learned earlier have forgotten: they neither share nor count
so older values are never read again and can be dropped

retrieve.q: Walk through day 6 of the trace (n = 6, delay = 2, forget = 4): what is added, what is popped, what is appended, and what is the answer?
answer: share was 1; add new[4] = 1 (C starts sharing): 2
popleft new[2] = 0 (nobody learned on day 2): still 2

retrieve.q: Re-summing the window each day gives the same answer. What does it cost at n = 1,000, forget = 1,000, and what does the running sum risk that re-summing doesn't?
answer: running sum: two updates per day, 2,997 operations
the running sum depends on reading new[−delay] before popping; an order bug corrupts every later day, whereas a re-sum recomputes from scratch

compare.q: Same container, different job. What does each deque hold, what leaves from the left and why, and which one can drop items from the right?
answer: monotonic deque: indices that could still be the window max; rolling DP: every value of the last forget days
left end: the index that slid out of the window (max) or the day that reached forget (DP)
only the monotonic deque pops from the right, discarding beaten values
the DP deque always has exactly forget entries; the monotonic one has at most k

compare.q: A rolling deque vs a full DP table: what property of the recurrence lets you throw rows away, and what do you lose when you do?
answer: the recurrence only looks back a bounded number of steps
so memory drops from O(n) to O(window)
you lose the history, so you can't reconstruct which choices led to the answer
if reconstruction is needed, keep the table (the path-reconstruction card's point)

predict.q: Set delay = 1 and forget = n (nobody forgets in time, everyone shares from the day after learning). For n = 10, how many people know the secret at the end, and what pattern does the count follow?
predict.answer: 512 = 2⁹. From day 2 on, everyone who knows shares with one new person each day, so the number who know doubles daily: 1, 2, 4, …, 2ⁿ⁻¹. That doubling is why the card's n = 1,000 answer has 301 digits and why person-by-person simulation is hopeless.

apply.task: Trace people_aware(4, 1, 3) by hand, writing share and the deque after each day, then run it. Then trace number_to_words(1000010): list each divmod and each appendleft.
apply.done: Your trace ends with the deque holding new[2..4] = 1, 2, 3 and the answer 6; the words come out as One Million Ten, with the thousands chunk skipped because it is 0.
apply.hint: With delay 1, day t adds new[t − 1]; with forget 3, day 4 pops new[1] = 1.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the 512, or the doubling pattern?
Could you explain why reading before popping matters, with a delay equal to forget?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: recurrence reach → window size, or window size → the answer being its sum?
Where else have you kept only the last few DP values (Fibonacci, climbing stairs)?
